text: The Year in Evolutionary Biology Challenges and prospects in genome-wide quantitative trait loci mapping of standing genetic variation in natural populations 1Department of Evolutionary Biology, Bielefeld University, Bielefeld, Germany. 2Department of Biology, Centre for Biodiversity Dynamics, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway Address for correspondence: Holger Schielzeth, Department of Evolutionary Biology, Bielefeld University, Morgenbreede 45, 33615 Bielefeld, Germany. holger.schielzeth@uni-bielefeld.de A considerable challenge in evolutionary genetics is to understand the genetic mechanisms that facilitate or impede evolutionary adaptation in natural populations. For this, we must understand the genetic loci contributing to trait variation and the selective forces acting on them. The decreased costs and increased feasibility of obtaining genotypic data on a large number of individuals have greatly facilitated gene mapping in natural populations, particularly because organisms whose genetics have been historically difficult to study are now within reach. Here we review the methods available to evolutionary ecologists interested in dissecting the genetic basis of traits in natural populations. Our focus lies on standing genetic variation in outbred populations. We present an overview of the current state of research in the field, covering studies on both plants and animals. We also draw attention to particular challenges associated with the discovery of quantitative trait loci and discuss parallels to studies on crops, livestock, and humans. Finally, we point to some likely future developments in genetic mapping studies.

Keywords: complex trait analysis; genetic architecture; genotype–phenotype map; pedigreed wild populations; quantitative trait loci; standing genetic variation Mapping standing genetic variation in natural populations Adaptive evolution is based on selection acting on genetic variants that segregate within populations. The statistical description of segregating genetic variationusingthetoolsofquantitativegenetics1 has been largely successful in predicting the response to selection in animal and plant breeding.2,3 However, quantitative genetics make the simplifying assumption that allelic effects are small and numerous (the infinitesimal model),1 and while this assumption is in many cases sufficiently robust to make predictions and inferences,4 it is not fully accurate because loci vary in their effects on trait variation. Moreover, quantitative genetics does not address the identity of the genes involved, the distribution of effect size across loci, the interactions among loci, or whether the segregating polymorphisms are regulatory or structural. These are all relevant aspects of the genetic architecture, and quantitative trait loci (QTL) mappingoffersthetoolsthatcanshedlightonthem.

The first applications of QTL mapping date back to the early 20th century, when Payne5 and Sax6 used monogenic traits as markers for mapping bristle number in Drosophila and seed weight size in the common bean, respectively. The start of the era of genome-wide QTL scans is marked by a seminal paper by Lander and Botstein in 1989, in which they presented the theoretical framework for interval mapping.7 Sincethenthepossibilitiesforidentifying causal genetic variants have substantially increased, facilitated by the plummeting costs of genotyping and the increased availability of genome sequences. Genetic mapping has been widely used by human geneticists for mapping disease susceptibility and other traits,8–10 as well as by livestock and crop breeders to improve breeding responses.2,3,11 QTL 35 Ann. QTL mapping in natural populations Schielzeth & Husby mapping has also been used extensively in model organisms such as mice, Drosophila, and Arabidopsis (see Refs. 12–14 for reviews). Our review here will focus on QTL mapping in natural populations of nonmodel organisms—a much more recent endeavor.

QTL mapping in natural populations targets within-population standing genetic variation (SGV) that affects trait variation (hereafter we use SGV in this sense of segregating polymorphisms affecting specific phenotypes). More detailed knowledge about SGV can lead to a better understanding of microevolutionary dynamics. First, the number and distribution of loci give an indication of the variants that are readily available for adaptation.15 Second, knowledge about QTL can be used for studying complex interactions, such as pleiotropic effects, genotype–environment interactions, and sex-specific effects.16 Third, selection on known QTL can be studied under natural conditions; selection analyses in different environmentsallowdistinguishingbetweenantagonistic pleiotropy and conditional neutrality of genetic variants in different environments.17 Fourth, QTL mapping can help identify unknown developmental, physiological, and biochemical pathways, and therefore serves as a hypothesis-generating enterprise for further analyses.16 Gene mapping in outbred nonmodel organisms has been hampered by the lack of genetic tools (in particular, availability of markers), but because of technological advances, this field has seen a growing interest during the last few years. Very few studies date back to the 1990s,18 and there were only a manageable number until 2003,19 but numbers have rapidly increased since. In contrast to studies on model organisms, there are challenges and constraints specific to QTL mapping in natural, outbred populations, in particular the fact that allele frequencies are unmanipulated.19,20 This has the unfavorable consequence that power is reduced, because loci under selection are expected to show an exponential distribution of allele frequencies with large-effect variants being uncommon.21 QTL mapping is a classical top-down genetic approach that starts with the phenotype and aims to map genetic variants linked to phenotypic variation. We here focus on genome-wide scans for genetic variants, to distinguish QTL analysis sensu strictofromassociationmappinginapriori–selected candidate genes. In some cases, good candidate genes of interest will be known from other (model) species, and these can be used in targeted association studies.22,23 Large-scale screens of candidate genes24,25 hold some promise for uncovering loci contributing to SGV. Nevertheless, candidate gene approaches are necessarily affected by the amount of prior knowledge, and we therefore focus here on an unbiased forward search for trait loci using whole-genome scans.

Any genome-wide QTL scan requires accurate and error-free genetic marker information distributed across the genome, as well as high-quality phenotypic information on hundreds if not thousands of individuals. The association between genotypes and phenotypes is typically analyzed by linear (mixed) models, with phenotypes treated as response variables and marker genotypes as predictors.

In the first part of this review, we present an overview of genome-wide mapping strategies for SGV, including a summary of studies on plants and animals that applied QTL searches in outbred populations. We aim to illustrate the array of possibilities and limitations when sampling from outbred populations. In the second part of the review, we cover more general aspects and challenges, and offer an outlook to potential future developments. We include some recent examples of studies that have been particularly successful in identifying QTL in natural populations.

All QTL mapping approaches require that marker allelesare in linkaged is equilibrium (LD) with causal genetic variants (trait loci) that influence the trait of interest. There are, however, important differences in how LD enters into the analysis. The most notable distinction can be made between linkage mapping, which exploits LD that runs in pedigrees, and association mapping (sometimes referred to as linkage disequilibrium mapping), which exploits historical population-wide LD (Fig. 1). Linkage and association mapping approaches can both be used for QTL detection in outbred populations. However, linkage mapping is more frequently applied when mapping in experimental crosses, a strategy that is efficient for detecting QTL but gives only partial information about SGV. Experimental linkage mapping using line or population crosses Linkage mapping in line crosses is the oldest5,6 and most widely used approach to QTL mapping. In experimental crosses, long-ranging LD between marker and trait loci is created experimentally in the mapping population.16,26 The key advantage of line crosses is that allele frequencies at marker and trait loci are equalized; this substantially increases power because all meioses are potentially informative for segregating QTL.20 The situation is radically different from pedigree linkage mapping in unmanipulated outbred populations, where many matings are uninformative because either marker or trait loci are homozygous in both parents.26 Experimental linkage mapping requires that parents differ considerably in their allele frequen- cies, ideally being fixed for alternative alleles at trait loci. There are two basic options for selecting parental lines that are suitable for mapping. One requires selective breeding, and hence experimentally created lines (experimental linkage mapping using line crosses), while the other uses naturally existing differences among divergent populations (experimental linkage mapping using population crosses).

Classic experimental linkage mapping is based on inbred lines that have been produced such that (nearly) all individuals from each line are homozygous at both trait and marker loci.16,26 The development of lines can be done by randomly capturing haplotypes from the base population in inbred lines either through self-fertilization or by repeated mating among full siblings from the same family. Alternatively, targeted local inbreeding at trait loci can be achieved by breeding selection lines, a strategy that is most efficient for mapping variants of large effect.

QTL mapping in natural populations Schielzeth & Husby QTL mapping is done in either the F2 or a B1 backcross generation. One option to increase resolution of mapping is to use recombinant inbred lines (RILs) that are created by continuously self-crossing F1 or F2 individuals.27 RILs consist of (nearly) genetically identical individuals, and each RIL captures a different set of recombinations from the original cross. Even more complicated lines, such as near-isogenic lines (NILs), co-isogenic lines, or chromosome-substitution lines, can be generated in some study systems.14,16,26 Although, in principle, such strategies could be used for mapping SGV in outbred populations of nonmodel species, this is usually hampered by practical limitations.

Each cross and each swarm of RILs captures only two haplotypes from the base population and thus does not represent the complete genetic variance in the base population as a whole.20,28 This might explain the low reproducibility of QTL peaks in different crosses, as in the case of Arabidopsis,29 and limits the informative value about SGV in general. However, suggestive loci can be genotyped in the base population in order to study natural allele frequenciesposthoc. Animprovedexperimentaldesignthat targets SGV may produce many inbred lines that can be crossed among each other, each targeting a subset of the alleles segregating in the population. Although multiple line crosses have been applied in model systems (partly with large joint efforts such as in mice30 or Arabidopsis31), we are not aware of any field-based study on a nonmodel organism that has used a large number of inbred lines.

A potential problem when creating experimental lines is differential loss of genetic variants due to selection or stochastic processes (e.g., 77% loss in Mimulus RILs32). This might impair the possibility that conclusions may be drawn about SGV. Furthermore, relating the QTL variance to the total phenotypic variance (as a standardized effect size) can be problematic because the phenotypic variance in the mapping population is likely to be reduced owing to environmental and genetic homogenization (but is often increased in species crosses33). It is therefore useful to relate the QTL variance to the variance in the parental generation.19 Although inbred line crosses are frequently used in model systems,12–14 there are relatively few studies that used line crosses for studying natural populations (Table 1), possibly because of the labor-intensive breeding process.

Experimental linkage mapping using population crosses. Linkage mapping in population crosses is often the fastest and most efficient way to perform QTL mapping because population crosses capitalize on naturally existing genetic difference between populations: local adaptation and drift have done the job of the experimenter. If populations are sufficiently divergent in allele frequencies at trait and marker loci, population crosses allow similar benefits as artificially created lines by raising minor allele frequencies in the mapping population (F2 or B1) to near 50%.

Population crosses provide insight into loci that have contributed to population divergence and thus onlyindirectlytoSGV.Thefocusisshiftedfromcontemporary microevolution to past processes of divergence and adaptation.34 Intraspecies crosses are closest to the goal of mapping SGV. Interspecies crosses are possible (and the distinction is somewhat arbitrary), but the longer the divergence time among populations, the less they are expected to tell us about contemporary SGV.

Interpopulation and ecotype crosses have been conducted in a variety of nonmodel organisms (Table 1), and a related line of research is the study of loci contributing to domestication in crosses between domesticated organisms and their wild ancestors.35,36 Most of the studies rely on a mapping population derived from a single population cross, but more comprehensive studies are beginning to emerge, at least in model systems such as Arabidopsis.37,38 Pedigree linkage mapping in outbred populations Pedigree-based linkage analyses use segregation within pedigrees for mapping and are now almost exclusively based on interval mapping.7 Interval mapping offers the distinct advantages that there is no bias toward the most variable marker showing the strongest signal39 and that QTL effect size and location can be separated.40 The main statistical and computational tools were developed in the early 1990s.41–45 Linkage maps are required for linkage mapping, because the genetic distance (recombination fraction) among markers is needed for estimating identity-by-descent (IBD) probabilities between marker loci. Pedigree-based linkage mapping can be conducted in general, multigenerational pedigrees, as well as in fragmented pedigrees of multiple core families. Fragmented pedigrees are typical for studies on humans, but similar data structures may also be available in many natural animal populations. Particular statistical tools can be used for analyzing multifamily full-sib data.51,52 The precision of the QTL location estimate is determined by the number of recombination events, and deep wellconnected pedigrees contain information on many meioses per individual and are powerful for mapping; but a larger number of families in shallower pedigrees will be equally suitable. Importantly, linkage between marker alleles and trait locus alleles can differ between families:28 M+T+/M−T−segregating in one family and M+T−/M−T+ in another (where M+/M−are two marker alleles and T+/T−are two trait locus alleles). This also implies that the analysis does not identify particular alleles that are associated with trait variation, unlike in an associationmapping approach.53 QTL that are inferred from linkage mapping are characteristics of the founder population. Phenotypes of offspring merely contribute breeding value information for segregating genetic variants present in founders. If pedigree-based linkage mapping is applied in natural populations, the population of founders must be representative of the base population as a whole. In some systems, for example, in many plant and fish species, it is possible to generate very large full-sib families, and a single full-sib family can sometimes be used for QTL mapping in outbred populations (Table 2). However, the generality of the findings will then be limited to the pair of founders.

The reliance on segregation within a pedigree constitutes the greatest strength, but also the greatest weakness, of linkage mapping. Markers are coinherited with trait loci even over large genomic distancesbecauserecombinationratesaretypicallylow. Hence, linkage mapping has relatively large power for mapping variants on scales of a few dozen centimorgans (cM)16 and requires comparatively few markers(althoughhighermarkerdensitysafeguards against misestimated IBD probabilities in cases of missing genotypes53). Unfortunately, these advantagestradeoffwithalackofresolution,whichresults in large QTL confidence intervals.16,45 Pedigree linkage mapping was first applied to natural populations in 2002 for mapping birth weight in red deer,54 and this was the only study to be included in a review of QTL mapping in natural populations from 2005.19 The situation has substantially changed in the last 10 years, with a number of studies using this approach, mostly in long-lived species, such as birds and mammals, that are less amenable to experimental linkage mapping (Table 3).

Association mapping Genome-wide association (GWA) mapping is an extension of early (local) association studies.55 Instead of mapping the trait in families as in linkage mapping, allele frequencies are compared at candidate loci with respect to the trait of interest. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) take advantage of LD between marker and trait loci that exists naturally within populations.56 The statistical tools for genome-wide analyses were developed in the 1990s57,58 in connection with increased marker densities. GWAS have since become the standard tool for gene mapping in human genetics, where they have identified mutations for a wide range of traits and diseases.59 Recently, GWAS are also starting to be employed in natural, outbred populations (Table 3). Owing to the increased ease in genotyping for a large number of markers, this method is likely to supplement and possibly replace linkage mapping approaches in the near future in ecological genetic studies. There are two reasons for this: (1) GWAS bypasses the need to follow many individuals and their relatives over many generations, as the analyses require no information on recombination within a pedigree; and (2) GWAS offer both increased power and resolution compared to a linkage analysis.60 The increased resolution is a direct consequence of utilizing historic recombination events accumulated over many generations. Detecting the effect of the markers on the phenotype can be tested using several different methods. In the simplest case of equally unrelated individuals and no population structure, single-locus association scans are based on regressing phenotypes on marker genotypes one locus at a time. The fact that loci are tested one by one requires an appropriate type I error control. This level will depend on the effective number of tests carried out and can be estimated in a number of different ways, includingstepwiseBonferroniandfalse-discoveryrate control,65,66 both of which can be overly stringent if some of the markers are in LD with each other.

Theabsenceofcrypticrelatednessandpopulation structure is often unrealistic, and naive mapping can therefore lead to increased rates of false positives. Population stratification therefore needs to be explicitly modeled to avoid spurious associations.67 This problem can be especially troublesome if both phenotypic and genetic differentiation varies with geographical distance. Several methods have been proposed to control for population stratification, but common to them is that they rely on fitting the genomic kinship matrix into a mixed-model framework.68–70 The kinship matrix captures both population structure and cryptic relatedness in the sample and is therefore an efficient way to reduce false-positive associations. By being marker based, the kinship matrix estimates realized relatedness, but it can potentially be replaced by the expected relatedness matrix inferred from a well-connected pedigree.

Admixture mapping Admixture mapping makes use of natural introgression in hybrid zones and, like association mapping, utilizes naturally occurring, population-wide patterns of LD.71,72 The analysis benefits from the increased LD and increased variation (genetic and phenotypic) in hybridizing populations with different degrees of backcrossing.72 An ideal mapping population for admixture mapping therefore harbors recent hybrids with far-ranging LD as well as advanced intercrosses or backcrosses that have accumulated recombinations over many generations. The difference in genetic composition between individuals potentially allows high-resolution QTL mapping with comparatively few markers, as compared to association mapping.72–74 In admixture mapping, marker information is used for estimating a hybrid index that describes the genome-wide degree of mixture among parental genomes for each individual.72 The analysis contrasts the genome-wide hybrid index with mixture at individual loci. If the locus-specific degree of mixing is larger or smaller than introgression in the remainder of the genome, this represents excess admixture. The basic mapping model fits locus-wise excess admixture as a predictor for the phenotype of interest.72,75 Similar to association mapping, linkage maps and an annotated genome are not required, but they greatly assist in interpreting the findings.71,72 Admixture mapping is tailored to mapping in natural systems where interbreeding takes place between species, subspecies, ecotypes, or any populations that are genetically sufficiently diverged from each other. The rather specific conditions of persistent admixture among sufficiently divergent parental lines make admixture mapping difficult to apply in many natural populations that do not hybridize. Nevertheless, admixture mapping has been successfully used for mapping variants for human diseases76–78 andinafewoutbrednonhumanorganisms (Table 3, with a few more examples of mapping in interspecies hybrid zones79,80).

Chromosomal heritabilities Evenrelativelywell-poweredassociationstudiesthat have used large number of markers and individuals have often only managed to explain a small amount of the heritability. This is perhaps best exemplified by human height, where QTL from GWAS explained only approximately 5% of the heritability.81 Yang et al. proposed to fit all markers simultaneously instead of testing the significance of markers individually,82 which should provide an unbiased estimate of the variance explained by the sum of all trait loci linked to markers. This expectation is indeed fulfilled for many traits,83 which is indicative of a polygenic basis, but there is also some variation around a linear relationship that suggests that, for some traits, some chromosomes contribute disproportionately.

While chromosomal heritabilities do not allow mapping to the level of individual loci, they can still provide inferences about the genetic architecture (and are therefore included here). Outlier chromosomes could potentially be interpreted as evidence against a strictly polygenic model.84,85 However, we would urge caution in using the relationship between chromosome size and proportion of variance explained to infer too much about the number of loci underlying trait variation. A disproportional contribution of a chromosome could result from either a QTL of large effect or the clustering of many loci of small effect on a single chromosome. Such clustering is not uncommon,38,86 and therefore even outlier chromosomes could be consistent with a polygenic model.

Agreement and disagreement between mapping strategies Association and pedigree linkage mapping are the most targeted approaches for studying SGV (Fig. 1). As we have outlined above, the two approaches have different benefits and drawbacks, with a fundamental trade-off between efficiency (in terms of marker density and sample size) and precision.53 To take full advantage of the data and increased power, it is therefore desirable to combine linkage mapping and associationmapping,astheyarecomplementaryapproaches with different strengths and weaknesses.36 Few studies have compared results from linkage and association mapping empirically for the same study population. A recent mapping study on clutch size and egg mass in a population of great tits found no genome-wide significant regions with either approach.87 Moreover, and somewhat surprising, nominally significant QTL regions detected in the linkage analysis did not match up with those from the association analysis.87 Similarly, a joint linkage and association-mapping approach to flowering time in Arabidopsis found that, while many QTL from the linkage analysis and the GWAS did align, there were also a number of associations from the GWAS that were not present in the linkage analysis.38 The discrepancy between results is surprising and requires an explanation. The major difference between the two approaches is the difference in LD structure. First, it is possible that linkage signals are composedofmultiplesmall-effectQTLthatindividuallyaretooweaktobedetectedbyassociationmap- ping. Second, rare variants of moderate/large effect may be poorly marked in an association study but may show up as segregating within families. However, if a trait locus is well marked by a marker locus, association mapping is more powerful by combining evidence across families.

A useful approach, therefore, is to combine linkage and association mapping as two confirmatory approaches (though these do not constitute independent replication if based on the same data set). For example, a disagreement might be caused by failure to control for population structure in an association study, thereby causing a false positive.38 When planning follow-up studies, it would be most promising to pursue associations that are identified by both approaches.

Choice of traits It has been suggested that heritability (i.e., the degree to which the phenotypic variation is influenced by heritable variation) affects the chance to discover QTL.88 While some studies report a positive correlation between QTL effect size and additive genetic variance for the same trait,30 there is in general no reason to expect that traits with a high proportion of additive genetic variance should harbor large-effect variants rather than many loci with small effects.89 An excellent illustration of this point is provided by GWAS on human height, where, despite a high heritability of around 0.8, each QTL analysis explains less than 1% of the phenotypic variance despite very large sample sizes.90 From a statistical viewpoint, what matters is a low amount of residual variance, not a high heritability per se; and if other known 45 Ann. Because most causal variants are likely to be of small effect, QTL analyses are very dependent on maximizing statistical power, but a direct link between heritability and the number and effect size of trait loci is not compelling.

A second consideration is whether traits systematically differ in their genetic architecture. The current empirical evidence is ambiguous and largely confounded with sample size. However, it is conceivable that traits that are intimately connected to biochemical pathways are likely to be influenced by fewer genes, and it might be easier to map important switches (trait loci) in such traits as compared to highly integrated traits. For example, it is likely that almost all loci contribute to an individual’s life span with small average effect.12 Specific causes of reduced life span, such as liver cancer, are likely to be influenced primarily by specific genes, in this case genesrelatedtoliverfunction,whicharepresumably fewer in number. Similarly, traits like the red color of the zebra finch beak might be closely linked to metabolic pathways related to carotenoid transport, andbeakmorphologymightbecloselylinkedtospecific growth factors: both traits are thus promising for QTL mapping.91,92 The generality of such considerations is speculative at the current stage, but it is nevertheless worthwhile to consider the choice of traits when planning a study.

Biased effect-size estimation A notoriously difficult issue is how to obtain accurate and unbiased estimation of effect sizes in scans for QTL. Whenever QTL discovery and effect-size estimation are conducted on the same data set, such that the effect-size estimation is conditional on significance thresholds, the estimates for the amount of variance explained by QTL are, on average, biased upwards. The overestimation of effect sizes, known as the Beavis effect in the context of QTL mapping,93,94 is a feature of conditional effect-size estimation after significance testing in general.95 This overestimation of effect size is caused by effects near the detection limit that only reach statistical significance if point estimates are comparatively large in the particular data set at hand. Unfortunately, QTL scans are always working at the detection limit, because most QTL have small to very small effects.96 Hence, sets of significant QTL will always be enriched for overestimated effects. Unfortunately, using a single sample it is impossible to determine if an estimated effect is truly large or if it was overestimated in the particular sample used.

Empirical data show a strong negative correlation between estimated effect size and sample size,26,85 which demonstrates that the Beavis effect is particularly problematic in studies with low power. Sample size thresholds, above which the Beavis effect is deemed to be less of an issue, have been suggested (e.g., N > 30020, N > 50094), but while increased sample size shifts the problem, it does not solve it completely. The Beavis effect is strongest at the detection limit, and larger sample sizes decrease the detection limit. This means that smaller effect variants will come into reach of significance, and the average effect size of significant QTL will still be overestimated, although more data will increase confidence in the estimates. Notably, when mapping in unmanipulated pedigrees, there is also internal heterogeneity in power, because of variation in allele frequencies and/or marker densities across the genome. This makes it even more problematic to define useful thresholds. Since the ultimate cause of theBeaviseffectisconditionaleffect-sizeestimation, theonlysustainablesolutioniseffect-sizeestimation at a priori defined loci in an independent sample. Unfortunately, replication and accurate effect-size estimation is particularly problematic in pedigree linkage analyses due to the difficulty in replicating the sampling design.

The overestimation of effect sizes has an intriguing and often overlooked consequence: replication studies of similar sample size will tend to result in an inflated number of false-negative findings. The inabilitytoreplicateinitiallysignificantfindingsowing to overoptimistic expectations concerning effect sizes is called the winner’s curse.97,98 Hence, somewhat counterintuitively, replication studies have to be designed larger than the initial study to avoid the riskoffalselyrejectingQTL.99,100 Unfortunately,this important point is easily forgotten.

Replication of a QTL signal could be done (1) using a different sample from the same population, (2) using a sample from a different population of the same species, (3) using a samplefrominadifferentspecies(comparativeQTL mapping103,104), or (4) ultimately, by demonstrating the mechanistic link using functional assays.102 There are constraints on replication imposed by the study system. For example, a pedigree linkage analysis in a natural population cannot be easily replicated in the same population because pedigree data often need years to be collected. A useful strategy that also generalizes the results is replication in a different but similar population.102 Replication of QTL results has proven difficult in humans, and the problems with reproducibility seem to stem mainly from four main issues:9 lack of control for population stratification and/or cryptic relatedness; differences in LD between marker and trait loci in different populations;105 differences in genetic structure between populations (genetic heterogeneity); and presence of genotype–genotype or genotype–environment interactions.9 Since some of the reasons are rooted in differences among populations and are therefore of biological relevance, it is advisable to first replicate the analysis in a population that is similar to the discovery sample, and it is important that the phenotype has been measured in a standardized way.102 Replication of QTL studies has thus far been relatively rare in natural populations of nonmodel organisms, although several studies contain internal replication in multiple independent samples.106,107 An impressive demonstration of replication has been achieved in ecotype crosses of three-spined sticklebacks, where QTL for pelvic spine structures were identified in a single cross108 and then replicated in multiple populations from the same geographic region109 and from different continents.110,111 Another instructive case is a candidate-gene approach applied to personality traits in great tits: the DRD4 gene was found to influence personality,112 a result that was replicated within the same population but not in others.113 This lack of replication has subsequently been shown not to be due to interpopulation differences in LD between the marker and trait locus.114 In addition, the mapping of horn-type polymorphism to chromosome 10 in Soay sheep has been replicated using linkage,115 GWA,116 and fine mapping.116 Strategies for fine mapping Confidence regions for QTL signals are typically large, in particular in linkage analyses, and usually cover dozens or hundreds of genes. A better functional understanding of trait-specific SGV requires a more fine-scaled mapping of genetic variants to evaluate if a QTL signal is caused by a single locus of large effect or if it constitutes the composite effect of multiple loci with small effect. It is not unusual for a single quantitative trait locus to decompose into multiplesmall-effectloci,possiblyevenspatiallyoffset from the original signal (ghost QTL).26,40 Fine mapping within pedigrees or line crosses requires a very large number of individuals, because LD blocks have to be broken up by recombination. Themarginalgainofadditionalgenerationsforlinkage mapping decreases,28 and extending a pedigree is therefore only occasionally a promising option. A follow-up by association mapping can therefore be an attractive choice.12 This requires a far larger numberofmarkers,butnotsuchadramaticincrease in sample sizes. The statistical power of association mappingcanbefurtherincreasedbylarge-scalephenotype screens with selective genotyping of extreme phenotypes or sequencing of the QTL region.20 A generally promising strategy is to combine QTL mapping with other approaches such as transcriptome profiling,117 population genomics,47,118 or comparative genomic119 approaches. Population genomics uses large-scale genotyping or resequencing of individuals within populations to identify regions of the genome that are unusually differentiated, but it does not focus on particular phenotypes, and it can be difficult to separate outlier loci thought to be under selection from demographic effects.47,120 Similarly, comparative genomics of divergent populations119 can also help to identify outlier loci of divergence but is again not specific to individual phenotypes. The success of such a positional candidate-gene strategy36 depends on the amount of knowledge from other species and is more likely to be successful if an annotated genome assemblyisavailableandifthestudyspeciesisclosely related to a model organism. Ultimately, the study of post hoc candidate genes has similar drawbacks as the a priori selection of candidate genes, because even if causal polymorphisms are identified in the candidate it will remain unclear if this is the only, or even the main, locus contributing to the initial QTL signal.

Some studies in natural populations have been successful in fine mapping QTL to the level of a single QTG or even single nucleoid polymorphisms (quantitative trait nucleotide, QTN) (Box 1). Most of these fine-mapping successes have been supported by evidence from other approaches, including population genomics and functional analyses. Admittedly,mostofthesuccessstoriesconcerntraits with a rather simple genetic architecture. Nevertheless, they nicely demonstrate how QTL mapping can help to elucidate the genotype–phenotype map.

Some lessons can be learned from the extensive experience with QTL mapping in humans, livestock, and crops. A particularly striking, and at first glance surprising, fact is that, despite substantial efforts and sample sizes in the hundreds of thousands, the QTL that have been identified explain only a small amount of the genetic variance, a phenomena coinedthemissingheritabilitymystery.122 Agoodexample is human height. The trait shows substantial heritable genetic variation that amounts to 80% of the phenotypic variants. Yet, even very large-scale association studies have identified about 180 loci that in sum explain only 10% of the phenotypic variance.123–126 Such findings have led some authors to have a pessimistic view on the future of QTL mapping.127,128 Replication and fine mapping have been moderately successful in model organisms and humans,129,130 but the causal functional details of complex traits have remained largely unknown, even in humans.4,130 Furthermore, the results from studies from model organisms are ambiguous with respecttothesharingofQTLacrosspopulationsand species with shared QTL among some populations and species,131 but not in other cases.29 The history of QTL studies in model organisms is characterized by widespread reports of large QTL in the initial phase, with smaller effect sizes and a more complex picture of quantitative genetic variation in later studies.96,129 It seems likely that QTL studies on outbred populations are in the process of repeating this history, which is indicated by trends expressed in recent reviews.46,85 Hence, the field of ecological genomics might ultimately also realize that most quantitative traits are governed by large numbers of loci with small effect, while large-effect variants are rare.96 This observation appears remarkably valid across a wide range of traits and species,30,129,130,132 even if exceptions do exist.133 Thus, the infinitesimal model might be surprisingly valid, and we cannot expect every QTL mapping effort to discover segregating large-effect variants.

As the costs of sequencing and genotyping continue to decrease, it will become increasingly feasible to use resequencing-based methods for QTL mapping. Resequencing will ensure that the causal variants are covered, which will solve the issue with low LD in association studies. However, it will be of little use when mapping in pedigrees, because linkage analyses are not limited by the linkage among markers but by the lack of recombination. Thus far, resequencing approaches have rarely been used for mapping SGV for fitness traits in natural populations, though a notable exception is the detection of candidate genes for adaptation to serpentine soil in Arabidopsis lyrata.134 More resequencing studies are on their way in other organisms, and this should yield important insights into the role of other genetic variants, such as insertions, deletions, inversions, and transposable elements in influencing trait variation in natural populations. Resequencing approaches will also aid QTL identification indirectly by boosting the potential for complementary analyses using population genomic and comparative genomic approaches.

In many species of conifers, the ability to release the seeds inside cones in response to an environmental trigger, such as wildfires, is an important adaptive trait, but the genetic basis behind this has not been known. Recently, Parchman et al.190 used high-throughput sequencing and a GWAS approach to remedy this situation. They sampled three populations of lodgepole pines from the Rocky Mountains and obtained a reference assembly from which they called more than 97,000 SNPs to be used in a GWAS on 98 individuals that were selected for unambiguous serotinous or nonserotinous phenotypes. Rather surprisingly, given the low number of markers (compared to the genome size) and individuals, the authors were able to detect 11 loci that were associated with serotiny, although the function of these loci was unknown.190 This study illustrates the possibilities offered by high-throughput sequencing and GWAS in a species with a huge genome (18,000–40,000 Mbp198) to detect genetic polymorphisms affecting fitness traits in natural populations.

Local adaptation and life-history evolution in yellow monkeyflowers (Mimulus guttatus) Yellow monkeyflowers are distributed throughout western North America and show two distinct ecotypes that are locally adapted to coastal and inland habitats. Ecotypes differ in many characteristics, including whether they are annual or perennial, time of flowering, plant height, and other morphological traits.159 Experimental linkage mapping in population crosses was used to uncover the genetic basis of traits contributing to local adaptation, including mapping of a suite of 20 morphological and life-history traits in 539 F2 individuals.159 However, most of the mapping was done using the possibility of constructing RILs in monkeyflowers. For example, Lowry et al.148 mapped salt tolerance in RILs and performed reciprocal transplant experiments to demonstrate the fitness benefit of the salt tolerance QTL. Furthermore, population crosses based on sampling from a larger geographical range helped to pinpoint an inversion polymorphism affecting flowering time, and reciprocal transplants demonstrated its contribution to local adaptation.199 Other work from the same group also shows the potential for studying selection on QTL under natural conditions. For example, key life-history traits have been found to be under spatially and temporally variable balancing selection.200 Adaptation to freshwater habitats in three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) Three-spined sticklebacks occur globally widespread in marine habitats but have colonized freshwater habitats on multiple independent occasions. Adaptations to freshwater habitats involve striking changes in morphology, most prominently in the loss of pelvic spines and armor plates. Both of these traits have been mapped in genome-wide linkage scans based on F2 population crosses between marine and benthic populations sampled from native habitats.108,172 The identification of the Eda locus as a QTG for armor plates was based on a positional candidate genes approach and validated by positional cloning and high-resolution association mapping.201 The initial linkage mapping of pelvic spines revealed one major and four minor QTL.108 The leading QTL signal was confirmed in multiple independent crosses, including some from independently derived populations.109,110 Fine mapping to a very small genomic region upstream of the Pitx1 gene was done by combining positional cloning, comparative genomics, expression analysis, and artificial breeding.108,111 Knowledge about the Eda QTG was used for studying pleiotropic effects under laboratory and selection-under-field conditions.149,202 Regressive evolution in the Mexican tetra (Astyanax mexicanus) The Mexican tetra is a central American fish species that has colonized cave habitats at least three times independently.203 Cave-dwelling populations are characterized by several regressive characters, most notably the loss of pigmentation and eye reduction. Clutch size in birds is a classical avian life-history trait, and numerous studies have demonstrated that clutch size is under selection and has a genetic basis,204 yet so far no genes influencing this trait are known from natural populations. To address this, Santure et al.87 genotyped 650 females using 5500 polymorphic great tit SNPs205 to map QTL for clutch size and egg mass using a combination of three approaches: chromosome partitioning, linkage analysis, and GWA mapping. Neither the linkage-mapping approach nor the GWAS were able to detect any genome-wide significant QTL, probably because power was too low to detect loci with the small effect sizes expected from a polygenic trait. This latter conclusion is supported by the fact that the amount of genetic variance on each chromosome and the size of the chromosome were strongly positively correlated, which is suggestive of a largely polygenic basis to these traits.87 The study illustrates that even with a relatively large sample size, it may be problematic to detect loci for ecologically important quantitative traits in natural populations. For the great tits, the search for clutch-size QTL continues.

The use of linkage-mapping and associationmapping studies on natural populations has successfully allowed the identification of loci important in adaptation, thereby providing greater insight into the mechanistic underpinnings of evolution. However, identifying the location of QTL is in itself only the first step toward this goal. What is needed is a mechanistic link between the genotype, phenotype, and fitness.138,139 The paucity of functional knowledge about most loci, even in model organisms, is a considerable obstacle in genotype–phenotype mapping. A recent extension to GWAS is to examine markers that are associated with a change in the variance between genotype classes instead of the mean, so-called variance GWAS.142 Mapping such variabilitycontrolling QTL (vQTL) can be particularly informative in studies on natural populations because genotype–environment interactions are expected to be common, something that may lead to differences in variance among genotypes. However, testing for vQTL places more demand on the data (i.e., requires large sample sizes), and they are therefore more difficult to detect than variants that change the mean phenotype. Moreover, there are a number of statistical concerns when testing for vQTL that practitioners need to be aware of. First, for many statistical distributions the mean and the variance are not independent, and care must therefore be taken to avoid scale artifacts. Statistical tests such as the Levene’s test for detecting variance heterogeneity are also sensitive to outliers, and transformation of the data to make it perfectly normal may be needed. Although, in theory, inverse normal transformation could be used to make data perfectly normal, this comes with its own set of caveats,143 and a recent high-profile paper examining vQTL in human height and body mass index (BMI),144 using the square of the values from an inverse normal transformation as phenotype, has generated some controversy.145,146 Nevertheless, given proper caution, this approach holds some promise for examining genotype–environment or genotype– genotype interactions in natural populations in the future once technical issues are overcome.147 It seems likely that the immediate next step in gene mapping in ecological genomics will be one of scale: more markers and more individuals will be scored to try to find the elusive QTL of quantitative traits. A particularly enticing prospect of this endeavor is measuring selection on the level of the QTL61,148–151 to better understand how traits can respond to selection and how genetic variance can be maintained in populations. This could be done either experimentally148 or by measuring fitness of individuals with known genotype.61,150 Fortunately, even if the causal genes remain anonymous, selection analyses can be successfully conducted by studyingselectionontheclosestmarkerlocus.152–155 Theadvanceintechnologyalsomeansthatamore diverse range of organisms can be studied, a process that will add important new knowledge about the genetic underpinnings of fitness-related traits in natural populations. Hopefully, such work will be pursued using a combination of approaches replicated across populations and followed, ultimately, by functional analyses and fitness assays. As more such studies accumulate, it should allow for a deeper and more complete understanding of the molecular mechanisms responsible for adaptation.
